Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Situation2: A significant community milestone is being marked, and attendees have travelled specifically to hear the imam's sermon.
Story: It was 2 a.m. when my phone buzzed, jolting me awake. On the other end, my closest friend’s voice trembled with grief—his father had just passed away. He needed me, not as an imam, but as the friend who had always listened, who had always been there. I sat on the edge of my bed, heart pounding, trying to offer comfort through the phone, but my mind kept drifting to the sermon I was to deliver in just a few hours. Today wasn’t just any Friday; it was the day our community would celebrate a milestone, and people had travelled from far and wide to hear my words. As an imam, I was expected to be composed, insightful, and present. As a friend, I was expected to be compassionate, attentive, and available. The weight of both roles pressed down on me, each demanding my full presence, each impossible to ignore. I felt torn, my loyalty and sense of duty pulling me in two directions, unsure which part of myself to give.
